```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(RdistNN)
```

`clate_dnn()` estimates conditional effects among compliers using a binary
instrument `A`, binary treatment `D` and supplied nuisance predictions. The
[paper](https://jakobjuergens.com/research/#orthogonal-inference-conditional-z)
defines the causal target and identifying assumptions. Reporting covariates
can be a subset of the controls used to obtain the nuisance predictions.

Observations at exactly equal represented selected-metric distance to a target
share the mean of their assigned rank weights
in both the reduced form and first stage, even when their outcomes or nuisance
predictions differ. Each deletion removes the actual row and redistributes
its remaining block's `n-1` weight-table mass over the survivors. This is a
ratio of two weighted signal averages, not an average of individual ratios.
The package warns that inference with persistent distance ties is not established.
See the [weight guide](dnn-weights.html#exact-distance-ties).

## Fit from a data frame

This synthetic example uses **oracle** predictions. The five nuisance
vectors are the instrument propensity and the outcome/treatment means in
each instrument arm. Arm indices refer to the instrument, not treatment.

```{r data}
demo <- clate_demo_data(n = 120, seed = 20261017, heterogeneous = TRUE)
d <- demo$data
targets <- rbind(c(.25, .25), c(.5, .5), c(.75, .75))
```

```{r fit}
fit <- clate_dnn(
  data = d, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), X0 = targets,
  y_col = "Y", d_col = "D", a_col = "A", e_col = "e_oracle",
  m_y0_col = "m_y0_oracle", m_y1_col = "m_y1_oracle",
  m_d0_col = "m_d0_oracle", m_d1_col = "m_d1_oracle",
  training = "oracle", row_ids = d$row_id, tuning_mode = "grid",
  return = c("W", "dx")
)
summary(fit)$coefficients
```

The default fit is retained while the grid compares alternative orders; it
does not select a preferred candidate. `training` records provenance and
fits no models. In an application, merge external predictions onto the
observations using stable IDs before fitting. IDs supplied to the estimator
cannot detect a prediction vector that was independently reordered.

For matrix inputs, pass the same vectors directly. Here the order is held
at the fitted default so the two calls can be compared:

```{r matrix-inputs}
X <- as.matrix(d[c("X1", "X2")])
fit_matrix <- clate_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets, Y = d$Y, D = d$D, A = d$A,
  e = d$e_oracle, m_y0 = d$m_y0_oracle, m_y1 = d$m_y1_oracle,
  m_d0 = d$m_d0_oracle, m_d1 = d$m_d1_oracle,
  s = fit$meta$s, se = FALSE
)
data.frame(data_frame = coef(fit), matrix = coef(fit_matrix))
```

Tibbles use the data-frame interface. All reporting covariates and prediction
vectors must be finite and aligned. Raw instrument propensities and treatment
predictions must lie in `[0,1]`. Propensities are clipped with `clip = 1e-8`
by default; clipping does not create overlap.

For a genuinely one-sided design, `one_sided = TRUE` permits omission of
`m_d0`; observed treatment must satisfy `D <= A`. The observed check cannot
establish the structural restriction. See `?clate_dnn` for its input rules.

## Read the first stage alongside the effect

```{r reporting}
fit$components
diagnostic <- as.data.frame(diagnostics(fit))
diagnostic[, c("target_id", "denominator", "denominator_se",
               "ratio_status", "wald_available")]
```

The numerator is the adjusted reduced form and the denominator is the
adjusted first stage. Their paired covariance enters ratio uncertainty.
`vcov(fit)` returns marginal ratio covariance matrices, one per profile;
it does not supply cross-profile covariance. These are estimator-scale
variances and must not be divided by effective sample size again.

An exactly zero first stage leaves the ratio undefined; finite negative
first stages retain a signed ratio. A finite estimate can have unavailable
Wald bounds. Inspect statuses and components before interpreting the output.
Weak local first stages can make Wald intervals unreliable. The
[inference guide](conditional-late-inference.html) explains these fields,
covariance scales and the separate experimental confidence-set helper.

## Supply two signals directly

If another workflow constructs the augmented signals, localize their means
with `affine_ratio_dnn()`. The package's signal constructor gives the same
inputs explicitly:

```{r paired-signals}
signals <- iv_augmented_signals(
  Y = d$Y, D = d$D, A = d$A, e = d$e_oracle,
  m_y0 = d$m_y0_oracle, m_y1 = d$m_y1_oracle,
  m_d0 = d$m_d0_oracle, m_d1 = d$m_d1_oracle
)
ratio <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets,
  numerator = signals$phi_y, denominator = signals$phi_d,
  s = fit$meta$s
)
data.frame(clate = coef(fit), paired_signals = coef(ratio))
```

Both components use common weights. Average the two signals before dividing;
observation-level signal ratios define a different statistic. Generic paired
signals carry no instrument record for overlap plots. Use the nuisance-based
CLATE fit when those diagnostics are needed.

## Plot and reuse the fit

With ggplot2 installed:

```{r plots, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width=7, fig.height=4.2}
plot(fit, style = "forest")
plot_overlap(fit, type = "mass")
```

Weight/kernel and influence views also use the shared plotting API. Keep
`"W"` for weight panels and `"dx"` for distance-based kernels. See
[Visualising fits](visualising-fits.html) for plot controls.

Extract one grid candidate or evaluate a new profile using retained signals:

```{r reuse}
candidate <- candidate_fit(fit, 1L)
coef(candidate)
predict(fit, x0 = c(.6, .4), interval = "confidence")
```

Neither operation refits nuisance learners. Saved fits contain observation-level
numeric values and inherit the data's sharing restrictions. `predict()`
relocalizes those frozen signals; it does not predict outcomes for new people.
For order controls, see [Kernel-order tuning](kernel-order-tuning.html).
For result fields, see [Notation and conventions](notation-and-conventions.html).
